title: The Options Pattern: Strongly Typed Configuration
description: Learn to use IOptions<T>, IOptionsMonitor<T>, and IOptionsSnapshot<T> to bind appsettings.json sections to typed C# classes.

terms.definition: A recommended ASP.NET Core pattern that binds configuration sections to plain C# classes and injects them via IOptions<T>.
A singleton, read-only snapshot of configuration that is populated at app startup and does not reload when the file changes.
A singleton that detects changes to the configuration source and fires callbacks when values are updated at runtime.
A scoped service that re-reads configuration on every HTTP request, useful for per-request changes.
Configuration APIs that map a JSON section to a C# class instance.

data.text: Raw `IConfiguration` string lookups like `_config["Api:Url"]` work, but they are error-prone: a misspelled key silently returns null at runtime. The **Options pattern** solves this by binding a configuration section to a plain C# class, giving you compile-time IntelliSense, validation, and a clean DI-friendly API.
Step 1 — Define a POCO Options Class
Create a plain C# class whose property names match the keys in your appsettings.json section. ASP.NET Core uses case-insensitive matching, so casing does not need to match exactly.

data.text: Step 2 — Register the Options Class in Program.cs
Call `Services.Configure<T>()` and pass the configuration section you want to bind. This registers `IOptions<T>`, `IOptionsMonitor<T>`, and `IOptionsSnapshot<T>` automatically.

data.content: Binding the ApiSettings section to the ApiSettings class using the options pattern

data.text: Step 3 — Inject IOptions<T> Into a Controller
Inject `IOptions<ApiSettings>` into any class that needs the configuration. Access values through the `.Value` property — with full IntelliSense support.

data.text: All three interfaces provide the same `T Value`, but they differ in when and how often the configuration is reloaded. Choosing the right one depends on whether you need live reloads and whether you're inside or outside a request scope.

cards.title: IOptions<T>
cards.description: A singleton, read-only snapshot populated once at startup. It does not detect file changes after the app starts.
cons: Does not reload on file change
All consumers see the same snapshot

cards.title: IOptionsMonitor<T>
cards.description: A singleton that watches for configuration changes and fires an OnChange callback whenever the source file is modified and saved.
pros: OnChange event lets you react to live updates
cons: Slightly more complex to set up

cards.title: IOptionsSnapshot<T>
cards.description: A scoped service that re-reads the configuration fresh for every HTTP request.
cons: Scoped — only available during an HTTP request

rows: Config may change while app is running

data.text: A misconfigured appsettings.json can cause runtime failures that are hard to diagnose. Use `IValidateOptions<T>` to validate options at startup and fail fast with a clear error message.

data.title: Validating ApiSettings — fail fast on bad config
data.content: Implementing IValidateOptions<T> to enforce rules on ApiSettings at startup

data.title: Fail fast at startup
data.text: Validation runs when the app starts. If appsettings.json has an invalid value, the app will not start and the console will show exactly which setting is wrong.
When you have multiple instances of the same options type — for example, several different external APIs — use **named options** to distinguish them by a string key.

data.title: Exercise: Bind and Validate Options
data.description: Practice the full options pattern workflow from appsettings.json to validated injection.
steps: Add a MailSettings section to appsettings.json with SmtpServer, Port, and UseSsl keys.
Create a MailSettings POCO class with matching properties.
Register the options in Program.cs using builder.Configuration.GetSection("MailSettings").
Add a MailSettingsValidator that requires SmtpServer and Port > 0.
Inject IOptions<MailSettings> into a ContactController and read the values.
data.expectedOutcome: A working options class, a registered validator, and a controller that receives fully typed configuration via DI with no string-key lookups.

items.question: Do I need to call AddOptions() before Configure<T>()?
items.answer: No. Configure<T>() registers all three options interfaces automatically. AddOptions() is only needed for advanced customization like named options or post-configuration.

items.question: Can IOptions<T> values change while the app is running?
items.answer: Only if you use IOptionsMonitor<T> or IOptionsSnapshot<T>. IOptions<T> is a one-time snapshot taken at startup.

items.question: What's the difference between Bind() and Configure<T>()?
items.answer: Configure<T>(section) is shorthand that calls Bind internally and registers the options. Use Bind() directly only when you need to configure options programmatically without a JSON source.

items.question: Can I combine multiple configuration sources for one options class?
items.answer: Yes. Use PostConfigure<T>() to apply additional settings after the initial bind, or layer sources (appsettings.json → appsettings.Production.json → environment variables) — ASP.NET Core merges them in order.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: The Options pattern replaces raw string-based IConfiguration lookups with typed C# classes.
IOptions<T> is a startup snapshot; IOptionsMonitor<T> reloads on change; IOptionsSnapshot<T> refreshes per request.
IValidateOptions<T> lets you enforce rules and fail fast at startup.
Named options (Configure<T>("name", section)) handle multiple instances of the same configuration type.
data.takeaway: Strongly typed configuration makes your app safer, more testable, and easier to refactor — stop using magic strings for settings.
